t109_ifs_p8: And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... At some point it’s a maze, and as my friend Pink, who has been healing her Dissociative Identity Disorder, explained, while it can be useful to have validation of the parts that one experiences, and ideas for how to work with them, it can also get overwhelming. People who are already overwhelmed can thus become more split up than before. I’ve seen many others echo this same evaluation, and it makes sense to me.
t109_sec_ifs:
How This Relates to IFS
Richard Schwartz, who developed Internal Family Systems (IFS), called one of his books No Bad Parts. Honor, understand and love every part, he says, and the protective ones are no exception, so “meet the protector first” would fit right in over there. That’s a lot of the overlap with this method, right there in the title.
My reparenting method diverges from IFS at an important point. The IFS Institute’s outline of the model says “everyone has a Self,” and that the Self “can and should lead,” once your parts stop “blending” with it. I emphasize the inner adult you build and practice occupying: Nurturer, Protector, and Leader, Guide, or Guru. That’s still one grown-up with three jobs, like back in The Chicken-and-Egg Problem.
Can’t find a calm, compassionate Self in there? Then borrow. One grown-up job at a time, from a friend who’ll play Protector for a night, or from something you do, like letting the phone ring when you know how that call goes (The Parent You Inherited again), until it’s yours.
Is a perfect Higher Self already waiting in there to be your guide or parent? I’d call that claim spiritual bypassing. I’ve had the Higher Self perspective myself, though. It’s a somewhat less subjective way of seeing things as working perfectly in reality, despite the ego’s illusions, which matches what people say about it. Where I part ways with IFS is the wisdom part. I don’t think the Higher Self has any specific wisdom. It’s a vantage point, where more wisdom and compassion can come up, but problems can also look like they were never problems at all from up there, and that can ironically lead instead to more foolish indifference.
You can see both sides of this see-saw in the guru types who supposedly embody their Higher Self. Anthony de Mello is an excellent example. He was a Jesuit priest who mixed stories from all kinds of traditions into his teaching on seeing through the ego’s traps and coming back to the Perfect Present. He also had a background as a psychotherapist who understood trauma-informed healing methods. He seemed to drift between the two opposite paradigms in a way that contradicted itself. And that bizarre contradiction is itself cited as “crazy wisdom” by apologists.
So inner child therapy draws on those higher vantage points more concretely. The inner Guide is the closest thing here to a Higher Self, and it has to work with the Nurturer and Protector and come after them. It can’t act like some transcendent authority that waves everything away. Most reparenting doesn’t do enough with the Guide, which is the opposite extreme from IFS, so I’m trying to bring together the best of both. IFS isn’t exactly one system, so I may be simplifying it here. It has its own branches and disputes, and that’s one more problem I’m trying to remedy by laying all this out systematically in this guide.
IFS calls these wounded young parts “exiles.” I find that pathologizing. I prefer to speak of a child who needs parenting and integration, rather than naming them by their wounded or excluded condition.
And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... At some point it’s a maze, and as my friend Pink, who has been healing her Dissociative Identity Disorder, explained, while it can be useful to have validation of the parts that one experiences, and ideas for how to work with them, it can also get overwhelming. People who are already overwhelmed can thus become more split up than before. I’ve seen many others echo this same evaluation, and it makes sense to me.
t109_photos_p2: While you look, notice any new feelings or urges, and any tightness or unusual feelings in your body, including the good ones. Use Pema Chödrön’s “feather touch” approach to gently bring some light and love to the edges of any contracted feelings. Is there something that younger you seems to want you to understand? Some of it you’ll remember yourself, and some of it you might even glean from talking to family/friends from then (“You hated that coat”). It might just be an inference you’re guessing from the picture, or perhaps it triggers an image or a dream. Or just nothing comes up. Ask what your little one needs from you now, and do a bit of it.
t109_sec_photos:
Use Childhood Photographs Gently
If picturing your little one feels like you’re just making them up, a real photo of you as a child can help, since there’s no face or posture to invent.
While you look, notice any new feelings or urges, and any tightness or unusual feelings in your body, including the good ones. Use Pema Chödrön’s “feather touch” approach to gently bring some light and love to the edges of any contracted feelings. Is there something that younger you seems to want you to understand? Some of it you’ll remember yourself, and some of it you might even glean from talking to family/friends from then (“You hated that coat”). It might just be an inference you’re guessing from the picture, or perhaps it triggers an image or a dream. Or just nothing comes up. Ask what your little one needs from you now, and do a bit of it.
We don’t need to ask it leading questions, like “Who abused me & how?” or “What memory is my body hiding?” Grilling one photo until a story shows up is a good way to get a story, but stories aren’t necessarily the truth, and even if they are accurate, the feelings beneath them are still more important. Memory is an amorphous thing, easily influenced by guided imagery and suggestions. Look at this study, for example, where people were shown a doctored photo of a childhood hot-air balloon ride they never took. Half of them actually started sorta remembering it. I’m sure you can relate.
A photo is just one moment that somebody picked and framed... not necessarily representative. Flipping thru an album may give different jolts in your body.
If you start to suspect someone of something serious, like abusing you, please don’t confront or accuse anyone based only on what came up here. You might be looking at the photo thinking, “That would explain so much.” Journal what came up and how it came up, and see if you can get support from someone level-headed who won’t lead you toward an answer.
Put the photo back in its drawer when you’re finished. If it starts tugging at you, so you keep going back to search it or you need to know for sure, or you’re getting overwhelmed, take a break from it right then. Settle yourself in the present to close out properly. Re-evaluation counseling always ends on this “Present Time” reminder. Can be as simple and silly as “Oh, Today is Monday, my favorite day of the week!”
t109_guard_p1: Whichever protective part showed up, try talking to it in the same Nurturer voice you meant for your little one. At some point you can ask that part, “What are you afraid would happen if you stepped back?” “Tell me what you remember, I’m listening.” works well here. It puts you into the role of the Nurturer, which alleviates the instinct to argue back. Usually your little one only comes forward after that part feels heard. Peek-a-boo!
t109_guard_p3: That part might say this will just be one more performance, and you’ll fool yourself again. That one can sting, because there could be something to it. Maybe you’ve fooled yourself before, and that part remembers. If you push past it, you might get exactly the performance it was afraid of. Even if you didn’t win an Emmy last year, that can look convincing, with the right words and maybe even tears, while nothing underneath feels any safer.
t109_guard_p4: That part doesn’t have to move out. It’s been living there way longer than the grown-up you. It can keep watch while you take one small step toward your little one, and I think watching is what it wants anyway, to find out if there’s a grown-up here now who could call it off if things got to be too much. It doesn’t have to be all or nothing, either. Maybe it would settle for a lighter cover for now, like blinds tilted open a crack, and let you peek out for a minute (ST-CA, section 9.3.4). If it says no, I’d listen. When it lets you, keep an eye on that part too, for any change at all.
t109_guard_p5: If it’s been calling all this stupid, it might turn out to be scared of getting its hopes up. I wouldn’t want to get mine up either. I’d tell it something like, “You don’t have to hope yet, I’ll keep coming back even when I mess up.” Sometimes it doesn’t say anything back for a while.
